answer.rationale: Finance has mandated an 18% cut; the low-cost vendor has already quoted a price that meets that mandate alone. Memory c2 records that moving primary supply to that same low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply last year, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate. That directly supports switching primary to meet the cost objective without historical signs of delivery or quality risk. Because the assembly line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and we only get one decision this cycle, I am not committing to a full primary switch on day 71. Instead, the guarded action is a small, time-boxed primary shift with the low-cost vendor covering the volume needed to hit the 18% mandate, while keeping the incumbent warm under a short extension as fallback. If the test performs against c2's pattern (clean onboarding, accurate invoicing, on-time delivery), the next review promotes it to full primary. The line's tight buffer means anything more aggressive risks delivery; anything less aggressive fails the mandate. Deferring (c5) only works when the renewal is non-critical and budget flexibility is the goal — here a decision is required and cost is the binding constraint, so deferral underperforms. Adding a second source (c3) improves resilience but does not, on its own, hit the 18% cut at the required scale inside one cycle and adds dual-sourcing overhead the buffer cannot absorb. Renewing incumbent (c1) preserves stability but does not meet the mandate. Negotiating (c4, c6) is useful as a parallel lever for the incumbent extension/backup terms, not as the primary cost action this cycle.
